extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal practitioners, and general readers interested in U.S. Supreme Court copyright decisions
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the Supreme Court's holding and reasoning on when district courts may award attorneys' fees under the Copyright Act, including the proper standard to apply to prevailing plaintiffs and prevailing defendants. Useful for understanding fee-shifting doctrine in U.S. copyright litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretionary nature of attorneys' fees under the Copyright Act (§505)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Copyright Act of 1976 authorizes, but does not require, the court to award attorneys' fees to 'the prevailing party'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute uses permissive language ('may' be awarded), so district courts have discretion whether to award a reasonable attorney's fee. The Court emphasized that this does not mean fees should be awarded automatically or routinely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same standard for prevailing plaintiffs and defendants
rubrics_metrics.description: In Fogerty, the Court held that such attorneys'-fees awards are discretionary, and that the same standards should be applied in the case of a prevailing plaintiff and a prevailing defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects a rule that treats prevailing plaintiffs and prevailing defendants differently; district courts should apply an evenhanded standard when determining fee awards in copyright cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ninth Circuit's prior differential standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Ninth Circuit standards, prevailing plaintiffs generally obtained attorneys' fees as a matter of course, but prevailing defendants had to show that the underlying suit was frivolous and brought in bad faith in order to recover fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The district court in Fogerty denied fees because it found Fantasy's suit was not frivolous or in bad faith; the Supreme Court overruled this circuit practice in favor of parity between plaintiffs and defendants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of Title VII analogy for fee-shifting
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court rejected the analogy between fee awards in copyright cases and civil rights (Title VII) cases, where prevailing plaintiffs often obtain fees as a matter of course while prevailing defendants recover only if the suit was frivolous or in bad faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Title VII approach was rooted in Congress treating civil rights plaintiffs as 'private attorneys general' who often cannot afford counsel; the Court found those considerations inapplicable to copyright litigation and therefore declined to import the Title VII standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy consideration: encourage meritorious defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court stressed it is just as important to encourage the litigation of meritorious defenses to copyright as it is to encourage the litigation of infringement claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because parties on both sides of copyright disputes range from 'corporate behemoths to starving artists,' fee policy should avoid creating disincentives to defend against weak or borderline claims; courts should consider the broader objectives of copyright law (encouraging creation and public availability) when deciding fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory interpretation: 'may' indicates non-mandatory awards
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court noted that the Copyright Act authorizes an exception to the usual American rule that parties bear their own costs, but the use of 'may' signals congressional intent to confer discretion rather than mandate fee awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Congress had intended attorneys' fees to be virtually mandatory, the statute would have said so; thus district courts should exercise case-specific discretion rather than award fees routinely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of circuit split and alternative approaches (e.g., Third Circuit 'evenhanded approach')
rubrics_metrics.description: There was a circuit split among the courts of appeals on standards for awarding attorneys' fees in copyright cases; for example, the Third Circuit favored an 'evenhanded approach'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court resolved the split by adopting parity between plaintiffs and defendants, endorsing an evenhanded discretionary standard and disfavoring rules that automatically favor one side.
